analysis.one_liner: Requires large hedge funds to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: Senator Grassley introduced it in May 2007, the Senate referred it to the Banking Committee, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law at the time, an investment adviser managing fewer than 15 clients could skip registering with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and hedge funds used that exemption to stay outside federal oversight no matter how big they got. This bill would close that door above a small size: any adviser managing more than $50 million or the money of more than 15 investors would have to register with the SEC, putting those funds under federal examination and disclosure rules. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors in larger hedge funds, who would gain the protections that come with SEC registration — disclosure of the fund's practices, books and records subject to federal inspection, and an examiner who can check for fraud and mismanagement. Ordinary people benefit indirectly too, since unregulated funds managing enormous sums can pose risks that spread to the wider financial system, as later events showed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrites the Investment Advisers Act exemption so that only advisers with $50 million or less in assets under management, no more than 15 investors, and no public holding-out as an adviser can avoid registration; larger funds would have to register with the SEC.
By counting investors in a pooled vehicle toward the 15-investor limit, the bill prevents hedge funds from claiming the small-adviser exemption while pooling unlimited money through one fund.
Registration under the Advisers Act brings funds under SEC examination authority, so a fund's practices and records would be subject to federal inspection rather than operating outside it.

analysis.who_pays: Hedge fund managers and other investment advisers managing more than $50 million or more than 15 investors, who would take on the cost and burden of SEC registration, disclosure, and examination. Investors in those funds could also face modest compliance costs passed through as fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hedge funds above $50 million or 15 investors

drawbacks.text: The bill only requires registration — it does not itself restrict what a registered fund may do with investors' money, and it leaves the smallest advisers under $50 million outside SEC oversight entirely.

Registration imposes real compliance costs on fund managers, and hedge funds generally serve wealthy, accredited investors and institutions rather than the general public, so the direct consumer protection for ordinary households is limited even though the systemic case is stronger.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: large pools of other people's money would stop operating entirely outside federal oversight, with the SEC able to examine records and detect fraud. The cost is compliance expense for fund managers and thinner protection for the smallest funds, which stay exempt. On balance the trade favors investors, and Congress ultimately imposed registration on these funds through later legislation after the 2008 financial crisis — evidence that the underlying concern was real.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Grassley introduced the bill, the Senate sent it to the Banking Committee the same day, and it never came up for a committee vote or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley introduced the Hedge Fund Registration Act of 2007 on May 15, 2007.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where its action history ends; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.
The bill attracted no cosponsors in the Senate.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hedge fund managers above the bill's size thresholds, who continued operating without SEC registration and examination for the rest of the Congress; smaller investors and anyone worried about unregulated pools of money lost the chance at federal oversight.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 15, 2007 and gave introductory remarks; the bill had no cosponsors.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; it remained referred to his committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Hedge fund industry
against.role: Fund managers benefiting from the existing registration exemption
against.what_they_did: The industry broadly opposed mandatory SEC registration of hedge funds during this period, and the bill progressed no further after referral.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls ever occurred and the bill drew no cosponsors, so no voting pattern exists to measure — the only recorded action is a lone Republican sponsor and a referral to a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and large investment advisers
industries.note: The bill would strip advisers managing over $50 million or over 15 investors of their SEC registration exemption, subjecting them to federal examination for the first time. Their interest in staying outside oversight ran against the interest of investors and the public in knowing what these funds were doing.

Advisers under $50 million with 15 or fewer investors would keep their exemption untouched, avoiding new compliance costs. This carve-out is exactly how the exemption works today, so the bill mainly targeted the large end of the business.
